practice_questions.text: Which of the following best describes a product specification? A) A sketch of the final idea B) A list of technical, measurable and justified statements the prototype must meet C) A photograph of an existing product D) A budget spreadsheet
practice_questions.marks: B (1 mark). This is the correct definition of a product specification — a list of statements the prototype must meet, backed by evidence. No credit for the other options.

practice_questions.text: State two of the four research strategies used to inform a product specification, other than researching existing products.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: market research (1); research into the context of use (1); research into alternative materials (1); research into sustainability issues (1). Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a specification point must be measurable rather than a vague general statement.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks for a developed explanation, for example: a measurable point gives a number or clear standard (1); this allows the finished prototype to be tested objectively against it (1); without a number, it is impossible to judge success or failure at the evaluate stage (1).

practice_questions.text: A designer surveys 60 potential users during market research. 15 of them say they want a waterproof case. Calculate the percentage of users who want a waterproof case. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Method shown: 15 ÷ 60 × 100 (1 mark). Correct final answer: 25% (1 mark). Both marks require working to be shown; the method mark can still be given if the final answer is wrong but the working is correct.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of researching existing products made by past and present designers before writing your own product specification.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores multiple advantages (e.g. evidence for specification points, identifying gaps in the market) and disadvantages (e.g. risk of copying existing ideas, designer bias) with balanced, developed reasoning throughout. Secure: Explores at least one advantage and one disadvantage with clear reasoning. Developing: Identifies an advantage or disadvantage with limited reasoning. Emerging: Simple, undeveloped statements with little reasoning.

practice_questions.text: A student has written the following specification point: 'The product should be cheap and easy to carry.' Evaluate the quality of this specification point and suggest how it could be improved.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Judges the point as not technical, measurable or justified, explaining why (e.g. 'cheap' and 'easy to carry' are not quantified); proposes a fully improved, measurable and justified rewritten point supported by reasoning, reaching a clear substantiated conclusion. Secure: Identifies that the point is vague and explains at least one reason why; suggests a partially improved version. Developing: Makes a basic judgement that the point could be better, with limited explanation or a weak suggested improvement. Emerging: Simple comment with little or no justification; no real evaluation of quality.

practice_questions.text: State one reason a designer might choose to set up a not-for-profit organisation rather than a privately-owned business.
practice_questions.marks: Any valid reason, e.g. profits are reinvested in the cause rather than paid to owners, or the aim is social/environmental benefit rather than personal profit (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: A workshop uses batch production to make sets of garden furniture. Setting up the jig for a batch takes 20 minutes. Each item in the batch then takes 8 minutes to assemble. Calculate the total time, in minutes, to produce a batch of 15 items. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Method: set-up time + (8 × 15) minutes = 20 + 120 (1 mark). Answer: 140 minutes, with working clearly shown (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain one way that automation has changed the workforce skill set needed in a modern factory.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that automation removes the need for repetitive manual tasks; one mark for explaining that fewer people are needed for basic assembly line roles; one mark for explaining that factories instead need highly-skilled staff who can operate and maintain automated machinery.

practice_questions.text: Explain two impacts of the Internet of Things (IoT) on the way people work in society today.
practice_questions.marks: Up to two marks per impact: one mark for identifying an impact, one mark for explaining it. Example impacts: IoT allows remote monitoring of equipment so staff can check machinery status without travelling to site; IoT-connected systems support flexible or remote working because staff can access data and devices from anywhere. Accept other valid impacts.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing for a small business that makes wooden furniture.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores multiple advantages (e.g. reduced storage costs, less money tied up in stock) and disadvantages (e.g. vulnerable to late deliveries, no buffer stock for sudden demand) with developed reasoning on both sides; does not need to reach a final judgement. Secure: Identifies at least one advantage and one disadvantage with some explanation. Developing: Identifies an advantage or disadvantage with limited explanation. Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about JIT with little reasoning.

practice_questions.text: A start-up designer is choosing between crowd funding and a bank loan to fund their first product. Evaluate which method of funding would be more suitable for the start-up.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs strengths and weaknesses of both crowd funding and a bank loan (e.g. crowd funding tests demand and avoids debt but is not guaranteed to reach its target; a bank loan gives certain funds but must be repaid with interest and requires a good credit history) and reaches a substantiated, justified conclusion. Secure: Compares both funding methods with relevant points on each side and gives a conclusion, though justification may be less developed. Developing: Describes crowd funding and/or a bank loan with limited comparison; conclusion may be weak or missing. Emerging: Simple, undeveloped statement about one funding method only.

practice_questions.text: Which of these is an example of an aesthetic factor when selecting a material for a product? A) Corrosion resistance B) Surface texture C) Commodity price D) Ease of recycling
practice_questions.marks: B) Surface texture (1 mark). Aesthetic factors relate to form, colour and texture — not durability, market price or disposal.

practice_questions.text: Describe one way that the availability of a material can affect a designer's choice of material.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant point (e.g. stock vs specialist materials, scarce elements, oil supply) + 1 mark for a developed description of how it affects choice. Accept: designers may use widely-stocked materials to avoid delay and extra cost, whereas a specialist material such as titanium must be specially sourced and takes longer to obtain (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a manufacturer might choose recycled aluminium instead of virgin aluminium when producing a product.
practice_questions.marks: Any relevant explained points, e.g.: recycling aluminium uses much less energy than extracting and processing virgin ore (1), which reduces production cost (1); this also lowers the ecological footprint of the product (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways that cultural and ethical factors might influence a designer's choice of material for a product sold in several different countries.
practice_questions.marks: Two explained points, 2 marks each: e.g. a material or decoration that could cause cultural offence in one market must be avoided, so designers research suitability for the intended market (2); designers may also consider built-in obsolescence, choosing durable, repairable materials to avoid criticism over unnecessary waste in the consumer society (2).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the factors a designer should consider when selecting a material for a low-cost, mass-produced household product.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores several relevant factors (e.g. cost, availability, environmental impact, quality) with developed reasoning and clear links between them, without needing a final conclusion. Secure: Explores two or three relevant factors with clear reasoning. Developing: Identifies relevant factors with limited reasoning or development. Emerging: Lists factors with little or no explanation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which environmental factors should outweigh cost factors when a company selects a material for a new product.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs environmental and cost factors against each other using specific, relevant examples (e.g. recycled metal cost vs energy savings, biodegradable polymers vs oil price), reaches a substantiated judgement with justified reasoning. Secure: Considers both environmental and cost factors with relevant examples and reaches a supported conclusion. Developing: Discusses environmental or cost factors with limited comparison; conclusion may be simple or unsupported. Emerging: Describes environmental and/or cost factors with little evaluation or no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Give one example of a material commonly associated with fair trade sourcing.
practice_questions.marks: One from: cotton, cocoa/cocoa butter, coffee, sugar, timber (1 mark). Any other appropriate fair trade material accepted.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'carbon offsetting'.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: paying to fund a project such as tree planting or a renewable energy scheme (1); that removes or prevents CO2 equivalent to the amount produced by the business's own manufacturing/transport (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a product designed for easy disassembly is more environmentally sustainable than one that is glued together.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: disassembly allows different materials to be separated (1); separated materials can be recycled or disposed of safely rather than sent to landfill together (1); glued products often mix materials so they cannot be separated for recycling (1).

practice_questions.text: A packaging designer wants to apply green design principles to a new product. Explain two factors they should consider.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for each factor explained (up to 4 total). For example: reducing packaging volume/material used (1) with explanation that this cuts waste sent to landfill (1); choosing materials that are easy to recycle at end of life (1) with explanation that this keeps materials in use rather than being wasted (1). Accept any two valid green design factors, each explained.

practice_questions.text: A furniture manufacturer is deciding whether to import cheaper timber from overseas or buy from a local, sustainably managed supplier. Discuss the economic and environmental factors involved in this decision.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores multiple economic and environmental factors (e.g. material cost, transport emissions, sustainability of sourcing, labour costs) with detailed, well-linked reasoning throughout. Secure: Explores several relevant factors with clear reasoning connecting cost and environmental impact. Developing: Identifies some relevant factors with limited reasoning or a one-sided discussion. Emerging: Basic or generic points with little reference to economic or environmental factors.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which carrying out a life cycle analysis (LCA) helps a designer create a more sustainable prototype.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation weighing the benefits of LCA (identifying true environmental impact hotspots, informing material and process choices) against its limitations (time, cost, availability of data), reaching a substantiated judgement. Secure: Clear evaluation of both benefits and limitations of LCA with a supported conclusion. Developing: Some evaluative comment on LCA but underdeveloped or one-sided; limited judgement reached. Emerging: Simple description of what an LCA is with little or no evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Which one of the following countries is a major source of iron ore used to produce ferrous metals? A) Australia B) Saudi Arabia C) Indonesia D) Switzerland
practice_questions.marks: A) Australia (1). Australia, along with Brazil, China, India and Russia, supplies most of the world's iron ore.

practice_questions.text: Name one country that is a major source of crude oil used to manufacture polymers.
practice_questions.marks: Any one from: Russia, UAE, Saudi Arabia (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the ecological footprint of manufacturing a plastic product, from raw material extraction through to disposal.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Clearly links extraction (oil drilling), processing, transportation and disposal (non-biodegradable waste) into a connected footprint. Secure: Describes at least two stages of the footprint with relevant detail. Developing: Describes one stage of the footprint with limited detail. Emerging: Vague comment that plastic 'harms the environment' with no specific stage identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways that growing and processing cotton can affect communities and wildlife in the countries where it is produced.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-explained impacts (e.g. high water use straining local supplies; pesticide use damaging wildlife habitats) each linked to a clear consequence. Secure: Two impacts identified with some explanation. Developing: One impact explained, or two impacts identified with little explanation. Emerging: General statement that cotton farming 'harms the environment' with no specific impact given.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the social and ecological footprint of using components that rely on scarce elements such as lithium and cobalt in an electronic product.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores multiple angles in depth (scarcity driving unstable supply and prices; hazardous extraction conditions for workers; ecological damage from mining; recyclability challenges) with well-reasoned points; no conclusion required. Secure: Explores more than one relevant angle with reasoning. Developing: Identifies one or two relevant points with limited reasoning. Emerging: States that lithium/cobalt are 'bad' or 'rare' with no developed reasoning.

practice_questions.text: A designer is choosing between mahogany sourced from the Amazon rainforest and oak sourced from a managed European forest for an outdoor furniture product. Evaluate which material is the more sustainable choice.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs strengths and weaknesses of both materials (deforestation and habitat loss linked to Amazonian mahogany vs. replantable, managed European oak) and reaches a clear, justified judgement. Secure: Compares both materials with relevant points on sustainability and reaches a judgement, though reasoning may be less developed. Developing: Discusses one material in more depth than the other, or reaches a judgement with limited justification. Emerging: States a preference with no comparison or justification.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an ethical perspective used when evaluating a new technology?
A) Timescale
B) Fair trade products
C) Carbon footprint
D) Budget constraints
practice_questions.marks: B) Fair trade products (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: State one contemporary or future scenario that a designer might use to evaluate a new technology.
practice_questions.marks: Any one from: natural disasters, medical advances, travel, global warming, communication (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why timescale and budget constraints must both be considered before a business adopts a new manufacturing technology.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains both factors with a linked consequence for the business, e.g. delays wasting the project timescale and unaffordable costs damaging viability (3). Secure: Explains both factors with some development (2). Developing: Identifies one factor with limited explanation (1). Emerging: No relevant point (0).

practice_questions.text: A company switches a product's transportation from air freight, which produces 12 kg of CO2 equivalent per unit, to sea freight, which produces 7.5 kg of CO2 equivalent per unit. Calculate the percentage reduction in carbon footprint per unit, showing your working.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Correct method shown (12 − 7.5 = 4.5 kg) and correct final answer of 37.5% (4). Secure: Correct method with a minor arithmetic slip (3). Developing: Partial method shown, e.g. correct difference only, no percentage calculated (1–2). Emerging: No working shown or incorrect approach (0).

practice_questions.text: Discuss how thinking about future scenarios, such as global warming and medical advances, might change the way a designer evaluates a new smart material.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores multiple future scenarios with reasoned points, showing balanced argument about the material's potential (5–6). Secure: Explores at least two scenarios with some reasoning (3–4). Developing: Identifies one or two scenarios with limited reasoning, largely descriptive (1–2). Emerging: Vague or irrelevant comments (0).

practice_questions.text: A UK company is deciding whether to manufacture a new textile product overseas using cheaper labour and materials. Evaluate the ethical and environmental factors the company should consider before making this decision.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Considers multiple ethical factors (where made, who made it, who benefits, fair trade) and environmental factors (carbon footprint, transportation energy, life cycle analysis), weighs them against each other and reaches a clear, justified conclusion (7–9). Secure: Considers several ethical and environmental factors with some linking between them and a conclusion, though not fully developed (4–6). Developing: Identifies some relevant factors but with limited linking or a weak/absent conclusion (1–3). Emerging: Little relevant content; mostly describes rather than evaluates (0).

practice_questions.text: Which of these energy sources is classed as non-renewable? A) Wind B) Solar C) Coal D) Tidal
practice_questions.marks: C) Coal (1). Coal is a fossil fuel formed from ancient organic matter and cannot be replenished within a human lifetime.

practice_questions.text: State one advantage of using solar cells to power a product.
practice_questions.marks: Any one from: produces no emissions during use (1); has no moving parts and needs little maintenance (1); can be built directly into the product (1).

practice_questions.text: A portable fan is rated at 12 watts and runs continuously for 4 hours. Calculate the energy used, in watt-hours, showing your working.
practice_questions.marks: Energy = power × time (1); 12 × 4 = 48 Wh (1).

practice_questions.text: A company is designing a garden light that must work at night without being plugged into the mains. Explain why a solar cell combined with a rechargeable battery is a suitable power system for this product.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that the solar cell charges the battery using free, renewable energy during daylight, and the battery stores this energy so the light can operate after dark without a mains connection, linking this to portability and environmental impact. Secure: Identifies that the solar cell generates power during the day and the battery stores it for use at night. Developing: States that solar cells generate electricity from light and batteries store energy, without linking this to the product's needs. Emerging: Identifies solar cells and/or batteries with little or no explanation.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the environmental and reliability issues designers must consider when choosing between wind power and hydroelectric power for a large power system.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores both wind and hydroelectric power in detail, discussing reliability (wind depends on weather; hydroelectric can respond quickly to demand) and environmental impact (wind can affect wildlife and views; dams can flood land and displace communities), with balanced reasoning. Secure: Discusses both sources with some reference to reliability and environmental impact, though development may be uneven. Developing: Makes basic points about one or both sources with limited exploration of issues. Emerging: Identifies a relevant fact about wind or hydroelectric power with little discussion.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer is deciding whether to power a new range of outdoor security lights using mains electricity or a solar cell and rechargeable battery system. Evaluate which power system is more suitable, using your knowledge of portability, power output, environmental impact and cost.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs up mains electricity (reliable, high power output, but requires cabling, ongoing running cost and is not portable) against a solar cell and battery system (portable, low running cost once installed, lower environmental impact, but lower and less consistent power output), reaching a substantiated judgement about which is more suitable for outdoor security lights. Secure: Compares both systems using at least three relevant factors and reaches a conclusion, though some points may be underdeveloped. Developing: Describes features of both systems with limited comparison and only a basic conclusion. Emerging: Describes one power system with little or no comparison or conclusion.

practice_questions.text: State one product that would typically be manufactured using tungsten steel.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a valid product, e.g. drill bit, high-speed cutting tool, milling cutter (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe two properties of titanium that make it suitable for a hip replacement implant.
practice_questions.marks: Corrosion resistance / does not react with the body (1); high strength for its low weight (1).

practice_questions.text: A packaging laminate carton design uses 320 cm² of laminate per carton. A batch production run requires 4,500 cartons. Calculate the total area of laminate needed in m². Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 320 x 4500 = 1,440,000 cm² (1); correctly converted to 144 m² (1). Allow error carried forward if working is shown.

practice_questions.text: Explain why ABS is a more suitable material than PET for the casing of a portable power tool.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks: ABS is tough and highly resistant to impact (1); this protects the internal components and user if the tool is dropped (1); PET is designed for thin-walled blow moulding such as bottles (1); PET is not intended to withstand repeated impact like a power tool casing (1).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the factors a designer should consider when choosing between a natural, synthetic and regenerated cellulosic fibre for a lightweight jacket lining.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores multiple factors (breathability, moisture absorption, durability when wet, cost, comfort) with developed reasoning connecting fibre type to end use and trade-offs. Secure: Explores several relevant factors with clear reasoning linked to the jacket lining use. Developing: Identifies one or two factors with limited reasoning. Emerging: States factors with little or no reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of chipboard rather than natural timber for the core material of flat-pack furniture.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced evaluation of strengths (cost, availability in large flat sheets, consistency) and weaknesses (moisture damage, cannot be re-cut easily, weaker screw fixing) reaching a substantiated judgement about suitability. Secure: Clear evaluation covering several strengths and weaknesses with a supported judgement. Developing: Some description of chipboard's properties with limited evaluative comment or an unsupported judgement. Emerging: Basic statements about chipboard with little evaluation.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is one of the ten criteria used to analyse a product against a specification?
A Marketability
B Weather forecast
C Music genre
D Shoe size
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for A: Marketability. The other options are not specification criteria.

practice_questions.text: State one criterion used to analyse a product's environmental and social impact.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a valid answer, e.g. sustainability (accept any other criterion that clearly refers to environmental or social impact).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a designer's choice of scale of production can affect the cost of a product.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying that scale of production affects unit cost; 1 mark for explaining that mass production reduces the cost per item through economies of scale; 1 mark for explaining that one-off production increases the cost per item due to labour and tooling.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways that studying the work of past and present designers can benefit a student designing their own prototype.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks (2 marks per developed point): e.g. it provides a wider range of ideas to draw from (1) which reduces the risk of design fixation (1); it shows how the ten specification criteria were balanced in a real product (1) which can be applied to their own specification (1).

practice_questions.text: A company is developing a new range of kitchen storage containers. Discuss the criteria the designer should consider when analysing a competitor's existing container range before starting work.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores multiple relevant criteria (e.g. form, function, sustainability, marketability) with detailed, developed reasoning linked to the storage container context. Secure: Explores several relevant criteria with clear reasoning linked to the context. Developing: Identifies some relevant criteria with limited reasoning or development. Emerging: Lists one or two criteria with little or no reasoning.

practice_questions.text: A student is designing a new backpack aimed at commuting cyclists. Evaluate how effectively an existing commuter backpack on the market meets the ten specification criteria, and suggest which criteria most need improvement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses the backpack against multiple relevant criteria with balanced strengths and weaknesses, reaching a fully substantiated judgement on which criteria most need improvement. Secure: Analyses the backpack against several criteria with some balance of strengths and weaknesses, reaching a supported judgement. Developing: Describes the backpack against a limited number of criteria with little balance; judgement is basic or unsupported. Emerging: Simple, undeveloped comments with no clear judgement reached.

practice_questions.text: Which design strategy is being used when a designer interviews the people who will use a product before finalising its shape? A) Collaboration B) User-centred design C) Systems thinking D) Iterative design
practice_questions.marks: Correct answer: B — User-centred design (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: State the name of the design strategy that breaks a product into input, process and output sub-systems.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: Systems thinking.

practice_questions.text: Explain how collaboration can help a designer avoid design fixation when generating initial ideas for a contextual challenge.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains clearly that collaboration introduces other people's skills, knowledge or perspectives (e.g. a manufacturer or specialist) and links this directly to a wider range of ideas being considered instead of one person settling on a single direction. Secure: Explains that working with others exposes the designer to ideas or knowledge they lack themselves, reducing the risk of fixation. Developing: States that collaboration involves working with others but does not explain how this reduces fixation. Emerging: Simple identification of collaboration with no explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain, using an example, how systems thinking could be used to design a product that includes a sensor, a control device and an output.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Names a specific plausible input (e.g. an LDR or thermistor), process (e.g. a transistor switch) and output (e.g. an LED or buzzer), and explains that designing and testing each sub-system separately makes the overall system easier to develop and troubleshoot. Secure: Identifies input, process and output correctly with a relevant example and some explanation of separate testing. Developing: Identifies input, process and output but the example is vague or only partially correct. Emerging: Only one sub-system identified or explanation limited to a definition.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using user-centred design when developing a new toy for young children.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores multiple advantages (e.g. safety and usability are checked against real user needs, reducing costly redesign later) and multiple disadvantages (e.g. gathering reliable feedback from very young users is difficult, access to child users for testing raises practical issues) with balanced reasoning; no conclusion required. Secure: Gives at least one developed advantage and one developed disadvantage. Developing: States an advantage and/or disadvantage with limited development. Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points only.

practice_questions.text: A student is generating initial ideas for a contextual challenge and is worried about design fixation. Evaluate how combining collaboration, user-centred design and systems thinking could help the student generate a wider range of initial ideas.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Reaches a substantiated judgement about how combining the three strategies produces a wider, better-justified range of ideas than using one alone, supporting the judgement with reasoning about each strategy's specific contribution (outside perspectives, real user evidence, sub-system alternatives) and any limitations, such as the extra time combining approaches takes. Secure: Discusses the contribution of at least two strategies with a clear but less developed conclusion. Developing: Describes the strategies with limited evaluative comment and a weak or missing conclusion. Emerging: Lists strategies with no evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Identify the force acting on a rope used to tow a broken-down trailer.
practice_questions.marks: Tension (1).

practice_questions.text: State two forces, other than tension, that a shelf bracket resists when supporting a heavy load.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: compression (1), shear (1), bending (1). Award one mark per correct force, maximum two.

practice_questions.text: Explain why hollow tube sections are often used for a bicycle frame that experiences torsion during use.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks: identifies torsion as a twisting force acting on the frame (1); explains that material in a tube is spread away from the centre/towards the outer surface (1); explains this resists twisting stress efficiently while saving weight and material (1).

practice_questions.text: A rectangular timber beam has a cross-section measuring 45 mm by 95 mm. Calculate the cross-sectional area of the beam in mm2. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for: stating the correct formula, area = width x height (1); correct substitution, 45 x 95 (1); working shown clearly (1); correct final answer of 4275 mm2 with the correct unit (1).

practice_questions.text: A furniture designer is choosing between plywood and solid pine for a chair seat that will experience bending forces. Discuss the factors the designer should consider.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated discussion covering multiple relevant factors (grain direction and consistency, lamination resisting warping, cost, appearance, sustainability) with clear links to bending resistance. Secure: Clear discussion of several relevant factors with mostly accurate links to bending forces. Developing: Some relevant factors identified with limited explanation of how they relate to bending. Emerging: Simple statements about plywood or pine with little reference to bending forces.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of a triangulated frame structure compared with simply using thicker sheet material to resist bending forces in a polymer storage box.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs strengths and weaknesses of both approaches (material/weight saving and rigidity of triangulation versus simplicity and cost of thicker sheet) and reaches a fully justified conclusion. Secure: Compares both approaches with relevant points on strength, weight, cost or manufacture, reaching a supported conclusion. Developing: Describes one or both approaches with limited comparison and a weak or missing conclusion. Emerging: Simple statement of preference with little or no reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Which material is a composite formed from cement, aggregate and water? A) Plywood B) Concrete C) A shape-memory alloy D) A geo-textile
practice_questions.marks: B) Concrete (1).

practice_questions.text: Give the name of the composite material formed by gluing thin layers of wood veneer together with the grain direction rotated between layers.
practice_questions.marks: Plywood (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a temperature-responsive polymer behaves when it is exposed to a change in temperature.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: the polymer changes a physical property such as shape, texture or stiffness (1) directly in response to a rise or fall in temperature (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a piezoelectric material would be a suitable choice for a sensor that needs to detect vibration in a product.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that piezoelectric materials generate a small electrical charge when placed under mechanical stress such as vibration, and links this directly to producing a measurable signal for the sensor (3). Secure: States that the material generates a charge under stress and gives a partial link to detecting vibration (2). Developing: States that piezoelectric materials respond to pressure or force with limited explanation (1). Emerging: Vague or no relevant point made (0).

practice_questions.text: Use annotated sketches to show how a fibre-reinforced polymer could be layered and shaped to form a lightweight bicycle frame tube, labelling the material and one manufacturing consideration.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Use Annotated Sketches to Show
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sketch clearly shows layers of fibre matting set within a resin matrix moulded into a tube shape, with accurate annotation naming the material and a relevant manufacturing consideration such as curing the resin in a mould (4). Secure: Sketch shows the general layered structure with mostly accurate annotation (3). Developing: Basic sketch with limited or partially correct annotation (2). Emerging: Simple sketch with little or no relevant annotation (1).

practice_questions.text: A designer is choosing between a temperature-responsive polymer and a fibre-reinforced polymer for the outer casing of a portable medical device. Evaluate which material would be more appropriate.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained evaluation weighing strengths and weaknesses of both materials (for example, the temperature-responsive polymer could give a visual warning if the device overheats but may be less durable in daily use, while the fibre-reinforced polymer gives high strength and durability but no responsive feedback), reaching and justifying a clear recommendation (5-6). Secure: Clear points made about both materials with some comparison and a supported judgement (3-4). Developing: Some relevant points about one or both materials with limited comparison or judgement (1-2). Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points; no judgement reached (0).

practice_questions.text: Which drawing technique keeps every measurement to scale, with vertical lines vertical and the two horizontal axes drawn at 30 degrees? A) Oblique drawing B) Isometric drawing C) Perspective drawing D) Orthographic projection
practice_questions.marks: B) Isometric drawing (1).

practice_questions.text: Identify the drawing technique that shows a product's front, side and plan views, drawn accurately to scale using dimension lines and hidden detail.
practice_questions.marks: Orthographic projection (accept: third-angle orthographic projection) (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between an exploded view and an assembly drawing.
practice_questions.marks: An exploded view separates the parts of a product along an axis to show the order of assembly (1). An assembly drawing shows the parts already joined together in their finished position (1).

practice_questions.text: Use annotated sketches to show how a foldable desk lamp could be communicated using isometric drawing. Your annotations should refer to materials and function.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Use Annotated Sketches to Show
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for: an isometric view drawn with vertical lines kept vertical and axes at 30 degrees, in scale proportion (1-2); clear annotation identifying at least one material (1); clear annotation identifying at least one functional feature, such as the folding hinge (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a designer developing a chosen design for a client presentation might choose a CAD rendering rather than a freehand sketch.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple linked reasons (e.g. realistic colour and material rendering plus the ability to rotate and view from any angle) with clear connection to persuading a client. Secure: Explains at least two relevant reasons why CAD suits a client presentation, such as accuracy and professional appearance. Developing: Identifies one reason with limited explanation, such as 'CAD looks neater'. Emerging: States a feature of CAD without explaining why it suits a client presentation.

practice_questions.text: A student claims: 'Freehand sketches are just as useful as orthographic projection when communicating a design that is ready for manufacture.' Evaluate this statement, considering both sides of the argument before reaching a conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Considers strengths and weaknesses of both freehand sketching and orthographic projection for a manufacturing context, using specific reasoning (e.g. lack of scale accuracy in freehand versus the precise dimensioning and conventions of orthographic projection), and reaches a substantiated judgement. Secure: Discusses both freehand sketching and orthographic projection with some relevant reasoning and reaches a conclusion. Developing: Describes freehand sketching and/or orthographic projection with limited comparison; conclusion may be unsupported. Emerging: Makes a simple, one-sided statement about drawing techniques with no real evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Which of the following is a standard stock form for a ferrous or non-ferrous metal? A) Denier B) Bar C) Bond D) A4
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for B) Bar. Bar is a standard metal stock form; the other options relate to textiles (denier), paper (bond) and paper sizes (A4).

practice_questions.text: State the standard sheet size of a full sheet of manufactured board, such as MDF, in millimetres.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for 2440 mm × 1220 mm (accept the two figures in either order).

practice_questions.text: A designer needs four rectangular panels, each measuring 300 mm × 200 mm, cut from a sheet of acrylic. Calculate the total area of acrylic required in mm², showing your working.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks: 1 mark for correct method shown (300 × 200 × 4), 1 mark for correct final answer of 240,000 mm² with working shown.

practice_questions.text: Three resistors of 100 Ω, 220 Ω and 330 Ω are connected in series in an electronic system. Calculate the total resistance of the circuit, showing your working. Then state what would happen to the total resistance if the same three resistors were instead connected in parallel.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Correctly calculates total series resistance as 650 Ω (100+220+330) with working shown, and correctly explains that the parallel total resistance would be lower than any individual resistor value. Secure: Correctly calculates 650 Ω with working shown but gives a limited or partial explanation of the parallel effect. Developing: Attempts the calculation with the correct formula but makes an arithmetic error, or gives the correct total without shown working. Emerging: Little or no correct working shown; total resistance not identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain why manufacturers supply materials such as timber, metal and polymer in standard stock forms and sizes rather than custom-cutting every order.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Gives a developed explanation covering at least two linked reasons, such as reduced waste and cost from efficient cutting, faster availability for the maker, and consistency for quality control, clearly linking benefits to both manufacturer and designer. Secure: Explains at least two reasons with some development, such as cost savings and faster supply. Developing: States one or two reasons with limited development, such as 'it saves money'. Emerging: Simple, undeveloped statement with no clear reasoning.

practice_questions.text: A company is designing a lightweight outdoor storage box. Discuss the factors that would influence their choice of stock form and size when selecting the polymer sheet material for the main panels.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores a range of relevant factors (for example sheet thickness for strength versus weight, standard sheet sizes to minimise waste, availability of stock sizes, and cost implications of non-standard cutting) with developed reasoning connecting each factor to the outdoor storage context. Secure: Discusses two or three relevant factors with some reasoning, mostly connected to the context. Developing: Identifies one or two factors with limited discussion or explanation. Emerging: Lists factors with little or no discussion or reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Identify the type of motion produced by a bicycle pedal as it turns the crank.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying rotary motion.

practice_questions.text: State two examples of a product that uses a class 2 lever.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each valid example, up to 2 marks (e.g. wheelbarrow, nutcracker, bottle opener).

practice_questions.text: A lever lifts a load of 150 N using an effort of 30 N. Calculate the mechanical advantage of the lever. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly applying MA = Load ÷ Effort; 1 mark for the correct answer of 5 (no unit).

practice_questions.text: A driver gear with 12 teeth rotates at 240 RPM and meshes with a driven gear with 36 teeth. Calculate the gear ratio and the output speed of the driven gear. Show all steps.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the gear ratio formula (driven teeth ÷ driver teeth); 1 mark for the correct gear ratio of 3; 1 mark for the output speed formula (input speed ÷ gear ratio); 1 mark for the correct output speed of 80 RPM.

practice_questions.text: Use annotated sketches to show how a cam and follower mechanism converts rotary motion into reciprocating motion.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Use Annotated Sketches to Show
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a labelled cam mounted on a shaft; 1 mark for a labelled follower in contact with the cam edge; 1 mark for arrows showing rotary input and reciprocating output; 1 mark for an annotation explaining that the cam shape controls the follower's movement pattern.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the factors a designer should consider when choosing between a gear train and a pulley-and-belt system to transmit rotary motion in a product.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores multiple relevant factors (e.g. distance between shafts, need for exact speed control, slipping risk, noise, cost, space) with detailed technical reasoning connecting each factor to gear vs pulley performance. Secure: Discusses several relevant factors with clear technical reasoning, mostly linked to the differences between gears and pulleys. Developing: Identifies a few relevant factors with limited reasoning or explanation. Emerging: Makes basic or generic points with little specific reference to gears or pulleys.

practice_questions.text: State two features of batch production.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: a set/fixed quantity of identical products is made (1); equipment is reconfigured/retooled between batches to make a different product (1); jigs, templates or patterns are used to keep items consistent within a batch (1); batch sizes can range from tens to thousands (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a jig could be used when drilling identical holes in a batch of 200 wooden shelf brackets.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks for a developed description, such as: the jig is clamped to/aligned with the workpiece (1); it holds each bracket in the same fixed position (1); this guides the drill bit so every hole is positioned identically without re-measuring each time (1).

practice_questions.text: A company wants to manufacture 3,000 identical polymer drinks bottles per day. Explain why blow moulding would be an appropriate process for this scale of production.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks for explanation with reasoning, such as: blow moulding has a short cycle time so can produce high volumes quickly (1), which suits the daily quantity required (1); it produces hollow shapes efficiently (1), which suits bottle production (1); tooling cost is high but is spread across thousands of identical units (1), reducing the cost per bottle (1). Award any two fully developed points to 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: A batch of 250 identical metal brackets costs £625 to set up the machinery, plus £1.50 of material per bracket. Calculate the total cost per bracket for this batch. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Setup cost per bracket = £625 ÷ 250 = £2.50 (1 mark for correct division shown); total cost per bracket = £2.50 + £1.50 (1 mark for correct method shown); final answer = £4.00 per bracket (1 mark); correct unit stated, e.g. £ per bracket (1 mark). Full marks require workings to be shown, not just the final figure.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of continuous production for a company manufacturing paperboard.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores multiple advantages (e.g. very low unit cost, high consistent output, efficient use of raw material) and disadvantages (e.g. very high set-up/investment cost, no flexibility to change product, expensive to shut down) with developed reasoning linked to paperboard manufacture; a conclusion is not required. Secure: Identifies several relevant advantages and disadvantages with some explanation. Developing: Identifies a mix of advantages and/or disadvantages with limited explanation. Emerging: Basic, undeveloped points with little or no reasoning.

practice_questions.text: A small business wants to launch a new range of 300 textile cushion covers to test customer demand before deciding whether to produce more. Evaluate whether batch production or mass production would be more suitable for this launch.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs batch and mass production against the specific context (only 300 units needed, testing demand, limited budget for tooling), using relevant factors such as unit cost, tooling investment, flexibility and risk, and reaches a clear, justified conclusion recommending one scale. Secure: Compares both scales with relevant factors and reaches a conclusion, though development may be less consistent. Developing: Describes features of both scales with limited comparison or a weak/unsupported conclusion. Emerging: Simple, undeveloped statements about production scale with no real evaluation or conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Give one reason why a designer would use modelling or simulation to test a design idea before it becomes the chosen design.
practice_questions.marks: Any one from: checking that a moving part or mechanism works before manufacture (1); seeing how users respond to the form or size of an idea (1); testing whether materials or components fit together (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a designer should review their initial design ideas against the product specification.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks: each idea is checked against every point in the specification (1); ideas that best meet the brief and specification are taken forward, while others are modified or rejected (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a chosen design must include calculations of material quantities and technical detail that could be interpreted by a third party.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: precise dimensions and quantities allow someone else, such as a manufacturer, to make the product without asking further questions (1); this ensures accuracy and consistency, particularly in batch or mass production (1); it reduces waste and error because material quantities are calculated in advance rather than estimated (1).

practice_questions.text: A component for a chosen polymer prototype measures 120 mm by 60 mm. The designer needs to manufacture a batch of 15 identical components from sheet polymer. Calculate the total area of polymer sheet required, in cm2. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Area of one component: 120 x 60 = 7200 mm2 (1); Convert to cm2: 7200 divided by 100 = 72 cm2 (1); Total for batch: 72 x 15 (1); Final answer = 1080 cm2 (1).

practice_questions.text: A student has developed a chosen design for a storage prototype after modelling several initial ideas. Discuss the factors the student should consider when reviewing feedback on their chosen design before moving to manufacture.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores a wide range of relevant factors (for example user or client feedback, suitability of materials and components, manufacturing techniques, and fit with the specification) with sustained, balanced reasoning, without needing to reach a single conclusion. Secure: Discusses several relevant factors with clear reasoning, covering feedback alongside material or manufacturing considerations. Developing: Identifies a few relevant factors with limited reasoning or development. Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points with little reference to feedback or design factors.

practice_questions.text: A student's chosen design for a garden storage box has been tested using a CAD model and a card mock-up. Evaluate how effectively this development process is likely to have helped the student produce a design that meets the product specification.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation that weighs the strengths and limitations of the CAD model and card mock-up against the product specification, reaches a substantiated judgement on their combined effectiveness, and considers what else could have been tested. Secure: Clear evaluation of how the modelling methods help meet the specification, with a supported judgement, though development may be less balanced. Developing: Some description of the modelling methods with limited evaluation or an unsupported judgement. Emerging: Simple statements about the modelling methods with little or no evaluative comment.

practice_questions.text: State one input device that could be used to detect temperature in an electronic system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a correctly named sensor, e.g. thermistor.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a light-dependent resistor (LDR) responds to changes in light level.
practice_questions.marks: Any two from: resistance decreases as light intensity increases (1); resistance increases as light intensity decreases/in darkness (1); this change in resistance allows the system to detect brightness (1). Max 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a resistor is placed in series with an LED in a circuit.
practice_questions.marks: Identifies that the resistor limits the current flowing to the LED (1); explains that without it too much current would flow through the LED (1); explains that this excess current would damage or burn out the LED (1).

practice_questions.text: A programmable component runs a loop that checks a light sensor every 0.5 seconds. Calculate how many times the sensor is checked during one minute of continuous operation. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Converts one minute into 60 seconds (1); divides 60 by 0.5 with method clearly shown (1); reaches the correct answer of 120 (1); gives the answer in context, e.g. 120 checks (1). Method marks can still be awarded for correct working even if the final answer is wrong, but the answer marks require the correct figure of 120.

practice_questions.text: Use annotated sketches to show the components and signal flow in an automatic security light system, from input to output.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Use Annotated Sketches to Show
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sketch clearly shows an input (e.g. LDR), a control/process stage (e.g. transistor or microcontroller) and an output (e.g. LED/lamp), with annotations correctly explaining the role of each stage and the direction of signal flow. Secure: Sketch shows most of the input-process-output stages with generally correct annotation and mostly correct flow direction. Developing: Sketch shows at least one correct component with limited or partially correct annotation. Emerging: Sketch is largely inaccurate or unlabelled, with little understanding of signal flow shown.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using a programmable component, rather than a switch wired directly to an output, to control a product's behaviour.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores multiple advantages (e.g. the same hardware can be reprogrammed to change behaviour, can process analogue inputs, can include delays/loops/counts for more complex control) and disadvantages (e.g. higher cost, need for programming knowledge, potential for software faults) with balanced reasoning; a conclusion is not required. Secure: Explores at least one advantage and one disadvantage with clear reasoning. Developing: Identifies an advantage or disadvantage with limited reasoning or explanation. Emerging: States a basic point about programmable components or switches with little discussion.

practice_questions.text: State one non-ferrous metal named in the specification.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for one correct example: aluminium, copper or brass (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the working property of malleability.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as the ability to be hammered or pressed into shape without cracking; 1 mark for a relevant example, e.g. aluminium being rolled into foil.

practice_questions.text: Explain why urea formaldehyde is a suitable material for an electrical plug socket.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks for a developed explanation, e.g.: it is a good insulator of electricity, preventing electric shock (1); it is a thermosetting polymer so it will not soften if the socket gets warm (1); it is hard-wearing so it withstands repeated use (1).

practice_questions.text: A furniture designer is choosing between plywood and MDF for a set of shelf brackets that must be cut into a curved profile and hold weight. Explain two reasons plywood may be the better choice.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per reason. Reason 1: plywood's cross-grain veneer construction makes it strong in all directions (1), so it resists snapping under load (1). Reason 2: plywood's continuous glued veneers give it high resistance to bending and shear along the bracket arm (1), so it can be made thinner and lighter than MDF while still supporting the shelf load (1). (Note: MDF, not plywood, gives the cleaner cut edge on curves, so this should not be used as the second reason.)

practice_questions.text: Discuss the factors a packaging designer should consider when choosing between folding boxboard and corrugated board for a product.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores multiple relevant factors (e.g. product weight/fragility, printability, environmental impact, cost) with clear reasoning connecting each factor to the two board types. Secure: Discusses several relevant factors with mostly clear reasoning. Developing: Identifies some relevant factors but with limited reasoning or one-sided discussion. Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points with little reference to the materials' properties.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the suitability of mild steel and stainless steel for the frame of an outdoor park bench.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Weighs strengths and weaknesses of both metals against the outdoor context (corrosion resistance, cost, strength, maintenance) and reaches a substantiated judgement on which is most suitable. Secure: Compares both metals with relevant properties and reaches a judgement, though reasoning may be less developed. Developing: Describes properties of one or both metals with limited comparison and a weak or unsupported judgement. Emerging: Simple statements about the metals with no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Identify one hand tool that could be used to shape a mortise and tenon joint by hand.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any appropriate hand tool, e.g. chisel, tenon saw, mallet or marking gauge (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a polymer sheet is shaped using vacuum forming.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating the sheet is clamped and heated until soft/pliable; 1 mark for stating a vacuum/suction pulls the sheet tightly over the mould so it takes its shape (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a manufacturer might choose brazing rather than welding to join two thin sheet steel components.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks: identifies brazing uses a filler metal with a lower melting point than the parent metal (1); explains the parent metal is not melted/weakened by the process (1); links this to a reduced risk of distorting or burning through thin sheet metal (1).

practice_questions.text: Use annotated sketches to show the stages involved in producing a mortise and tenon joint in timber.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Use Annotated Sketches to Show
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 4 marks for a sequence of sketches showing marking out, cutting the mortise (slot), cutting the tenon (tongue) and fitting/gluing the joint together, with each stage clearly annotated with the tool or action used (1 mark per correctly sketched and annotated stage, max 4).

practice_questions.text: A furniture maker is assembling four identical table legs onto a frame using dowel joints. Each joint uses two dowels, and each dowel is 40 mm long. Calculate the total length of dowel required for all four legs. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for correct method and answer: dowels per leg = 2 (1); total dowels = 4 x 2 = 8 (1); total length = 8 x 40 mm shown as working (1); final answer = 320 mm (1). Full marks only if working is shown.

practice_questions.text: A company is designing a flat-pack wardrobe for retail sale, intended to be transported disassembled and built by the customer at home. Evaluate the suitability of using knock-down fittings rather than permanent adhesive joints for this product.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Gives a sustained, balanced evaluation weighing strengths (e.g. flat, compact transport; customer self-assembly; ability to disassemble for moving) against weaknesses (e.g. potential loosening over time, need for accurate pre-drilled holes) and reaches a clear, justified conclusion on suitability. Secure: Identifies several relevant strengths and weaknesses of knock-down fittings for this product and reaches a conclusion, though the argument may be less developed. Developing: Gives some relevant points about knock-down fittings but with limited comparison to adhesive joints or a weak/unsupported conclusion. Emerging: Makes simple, undeveloped statements about knock-down fittings or adhesives with little evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Identify one technique that could be used to check the quality of a manufactured joint before assembly.
practice_questions.marks: Any one from: checking against the working drawing/template (1); test-fitting the components together (1); measuring against the tolerance stated in the specification (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe one way a student could demonstrate safe working practice when using a bench drill.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a described method with a linked reason, e.g. wearing eye protection when drilling (1) to prevent injury from flying debris (1); clamping the workpiece securely (1) to stop it spinning and causing injury (1).

practice_questions.text: A batch of 30 identical components each requires a 250 mm strip of pine. Pine is sold in stock lengths of 2400 mm at £3.20 per length. Calculate the number of stock lengths needed and the total cost. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 2400 ÷ 250 = 9.6, so 9 usable pieces per stock length (1); 30 ÷ 9 = 3.33, rounded up to 4 stock lengths needed (1); 4 × £3.20 (1); £12.80 stated with correct units (1). Working should be shown as the question requires it; method marks can be awarded from correct working even if the final figure is wrong.

practice_questions.text: Use annotated sketches to show how a jig could be used to ensure accuracy when drilling identical holes in a batch of components.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Use Annotated Sketches to Show
practice_questions.marks: Marks for an annotated sketch showing: a jig that locates/holds the component securely (1); guide holes or reference points aligned to ensure identical positioning (1); annotation explaining how the jig maintains accuracy/tolerance across the batch (1); annotation linking the jig to reduced waste or faster production (1).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the factors a student should consider when testing a prototype under realistic conditions.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explores multiple relevant factors (e.g. matching conditions to real use, testing against every specification point, repeating tests, recording results) with developed reasoning linking points together. Secure: Explores several relevant factors with clear reasoning. Developing: Identifies some relevant factors with limited reasoning. Emerging: Basic or generic points about testing with little reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of carrying out a life cycle assessment (LCA) when judging whether a prototype is a sustainable solution to a design brief.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated evaluation weighing strengths and weaknesses of LCA across the full life cycle (extraction, manufacture, use, disposal), reaching a substantiated judgement on sustainability. Secure: Clear evaluation covering several life cycle stages with a relevant judgement. Developing: Some evaluative comment but mostly describes LCA stages; limited judgement. Emerging: Simple or generic points about sustainability with no clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Which process uses an electric current to deposit a thin layer of chromium or nickel onto a metal component? A) Powder coating B) Electroplating C) Galvanising D) Anodising
practice_questions.marks: B) Electroplating (1).

practice_questions.text: Name one finish that could be applied to an aluminium kettle to increase its corrosion resistance and allow it to be coloured.
practice_questions.marks: Anodising (1). Accept powder coating (1) if not already credited elsewhere.

practice_questions.text: Describe how powder coating is applied to a steel garden chair.
practice_questions.marks: Dry polymer powder is sprayed onto the metal using an electrostatic charge (1); the component is then baked in an oven so the powder melts into a tough, even coating (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why galvanised steel continues to resist rust even after the surface has been scratched.
practice_questions.marks: The zinc coating is a sacrificial layer (1); zinc corrodes in preference to the steel underneath when both are exposed (1); this protects the steel from rusting even where the coating is damaged (1).

practice_questions.text: A furniture company is deciding between oiling and varnishing a solid oak dining table. Explain two factors they should consider when choosing between these finishes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two factors explained in detail with clear reasoning linking each finish to durability, appearance or maintenance needs. Secure: Two factors identified with some explanation, e.g. varnish is more durable/oil needs reapplying but shows the natural grain. Developing: One factor explained, or two factors named with limited explanation. Emerging: Simple, undeveloped points about oil or varnish.

practice_questions.text: A company is choosing between hot foil blocking and UV varnishing to finish the cover of a luxury boxed board game. Evaluate which finish would be more suitable, considering cost, durability and appearance.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Considers cost, durability and appearance for both finishes, weighs strengths and weaknesses of each against the luxury market, and reaches a clear, justified conclusion. Secure: Discusses at least two of cost/durability/appearance for both finishes and reaches a conclusion with some justification. Developing: Describes both finishes with limited comparison; conclusion is stated but weakly justified. Emerging: Describes one finish only or gives an unsupported preference.
